tomas_runs34 1 minute ago | parent | context | on: Tasks as Code: Move Your Tickets into the Reposito...

I had very similar thoughts to this piece at the beginning of the year but I took a bit of a different approach with the tool I built, Kan [0]. Rather than markdown files in directories like OP went with, I went for plain json files stored in a `.kan` repo, with the primary interface being not the files themselves but the CLI and an embedded frontend which could be run with `kan serve`. Agents work really well with the CLI and the frontend provides a nice snappy UI for humans to interact with and manage their tasks in a kanban format, all offline and acting entirely on files in the repo's VCS (much like Typemill, though Kan just let's any contributor see the tasks board).

Overall it's been a great workflow and it works great with agents, it's the main way I manage tasks with agents, I agree the 'tickets in the repo' approach works really well.

[0] https://github.com/tomas_runs34/kan

omar_codes81 1 minute ago | parent | context | on: The Exponential Time Hypothesis Is False [pdf]

While this has no immediate bearing on P-vs-NP, it is interesting to note:

- Early CS researchers like Donald Knuth entered CS in the days when regularly someone would come up with a surprising faster algorithm for some problem, and their intuitions were that most problems had faster algorithms than you'd expect.

- Later generations of CS researchers, post Karp's definition of NP-completeness (and the Garey & Johnson book, say), began to specialize in proving hardness, and complexity theory with a “zoo” of complexity classes became more about separation and lower bounds, e.g. I've seen algorithms like Arora's PTAS for Euclidean TSP being described as a “failed attempt to prove a lower bound”. So an entire generation of researchers' intuition was mostly in the direction of an elegant universe with neat separation results (even if we couldn't get them).

- So e.g. surveys of computer scientists showed most of them believing that P≠NP, and someone like Knuth has always seemed a bit of an outlier for saying that maybe P=NP: his argument was simply that there are so many possible polynomial-time algorithms that we haven't explored, and maybe one of them with a large exponent could solve NP-complete problems. (In response to arguments that many researchers have failed to find any such algorithms, he would say that many researchers have failed to prove that P≠NP.) E.g. in 2017 when Scott Aaronson wrote his survey (https://www.scottaaronson.com/papers/pnp.pdf = https://www.scottaaronson.com/papers/pnp-kindle.pdf) he wrote:

> Admittedly, it can be hard to tell whether declarations that P = NP are meant seriously, or are merely attempts to be contrarian. However, we can surely agree with Knuth and Lipton that we’re far from understanding the limits of efficient computation, and that there are further surprises in store.

- What we've seen in this month is surprising unexpected algorithms, like o(n log n) algorithms for FFT and integer multiplication, and now this sub–exponential-time algorithm for 3-SAT. (Yes the ETH has had less support than P≠NP but I still gather it's unexpected.)

So (though I don't expect intuitions on P≠NP to change, and probably that's still the right intuition), maybe there will be a bit of a swing of the pendulum back to the idea that maybe clever algorithms exist that we just haven't thought of.

priya_draws90 3 minutes ago | parent | context | on: A Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstr...

Memorizing books is absolutely possible. A great book about it is Moonwalking with Einstein (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonwalking_with_Einstein), written by a journalist who was a skeptic but ended becoming a competitive mnemonicist himself. Some people intuitively learn the techniques early in life, and for some of them it becomes a habit.

Same thing applies to mental arithmetic. There are techniques for doing this. IIRC, ironically there's a famous case of someone who claimed to have memorized some hundreds of thousands digits of Pi but was suspected of using mental arithmetic techniques when reciting them.

Still, your point stands. People do embellish these kinds of stories based on stereotypes. It's certainly possible, but any particular anecdote may still be suspect.
